title: Fingertip Pulse Oximeters at Home: How to Get a Good Reading and When to Call the Doctor
subtitle: A small clip-on gadget can estimate your oxygen level and pulse, as long as you know how to use it and what the number can and cannot tell you.
excerpt: Pulse oximeters are small and simple to use, but a home reading is an estimate, not a diagnosis. Here is how to take a steadier reading, what throws it off and what to look for when you buy.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: Many people bought a fingertip pulse oximeter during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the FDA. These small clips go on a fingertip and show two numbers: an estimate of your oxygen level and your pulse.

For some people, especially those whose doctor has asked them to keep an eye on their oxygen, that quick check can be reassuring. For others, the number can cause more worry than help. This guide explains what these devices do, what affects their accuracy and what to look for if you decide to buy one.
According to the FDA, the device clips onto a fingertip and estimates your oxygen level and your pulse. The oxygen number is often called SpO2. The key word is estimate.

The National Library of Medicine's MedlinePlus Magazine says a reading of 90% may correspond to a true level somewhere between 86% and 94%. Consumer Reports has said that home pulse oximeters are not as accurate as those used in medical settings, though we have only seen that in a brief excerpt.
Not all oximeters are reviewed by the FDA

This surprises many shoppers. The FDA says that over-the-counter oximeters sold in stores and online do not go through FDA review and are not intended for medical purposes. MedlinePlus Magazine adds that the FDA reviews accuracy only for prescription devices. The National Council on Aging recommends choosing a model that is FDA 510(k) cleared or FDA approved.
What can throw off a reading

Several things can affect accuracy: poor circulation, cold hands, skin thickness, skin temperature, current tobacco use, fingernail polish and a finger that is moving. The FDA also says current evidence suggests some accuracy differences between people with lighter and darker skin. That is one more reason to pay attention to how you feel, not just the number.

items: FDA clearance: look for the words FDA cleared on the product page. If a listing does not say, ask the seller for the clearance number before you buy.
Ongoing fees: neither of the product pages we checked showed a subscription, but confirm on any page before you order.
A screen you can read: look at the product photos and description for screen size and display options. The Innovo below has a rotating screen.
Batteries: check which kind the model uses and how you will replace them.
Compare prices: the same model can sell for different amounts at different stores, so it pays to shop around.
Returns and checkout rules: read the return policy, and note that some medical suppliers ask you to set up a verified account before checking out.

sections.content: A few simple habits help. The FDA suggests making sure your hand is warm and relaxed, and holding it below the level of your heart. Sit still and keep the finger with the oximeter from moving. Take off nail polish on that finger first.

If your doctor has asked you to track your oxygen, jot down the number along with how you are feeling. The FDA says to keep track of your symptoms alongside the number. Bring your notes to appointments. If you use an oximeter for a serious condition, follow your own doctor's instructions rather than relying on a single number.
"Contact a health care provider if you are concerned about the pulse oximeter reading." — U.S. Food and Drug Administration, "Pulse Oximeter Basics"

A pulse oximeter cannot diagnose anything, and it is not an early warning system for heart or lung problems in people who feel well. Yale Medicine reports that physicians disagree about whether people at home need one, so ask your doctor whether it makes sense for you. If you think your oxygen is low, see a doctor. If you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or a bluish tint to your lips or skin, do not wait for a number. Call a doctor or your emergency number (this is general advice, not from the sources above).
sections.label: Good to Know

sections.content: Used with care, a fingertip oximeter is one more piece of information, alongside how you feel. Keep your hands warm, sit still, pay attention to your symptoms and pick up the phone when something seems off. Your doctor is the best person to tell you what your numbers mean.

products.name: Nonin Onyx Vantage 9590 Fingertip Pulse Oximeter, Black
products.blurb: Suits people who want a model the page describes as FDA cleared for adult and pediatric oxygen spot checks, with no subscription shown. Prices for this model may differ at other sellers, and we did not check those listings. This retailer requires a verified account for some items.

products.name: Innovo iP900AP Deluxe Fingertip Pulse Oximeter
products.blurb: A lower-cost choice with a rotating screen that shows oxygen level, pulse rate and perfusion index (a gauge of blood flow at the fingertip), plus an audible alarm. The listing does not state FDA clearance, so ask the seller. We could not confirm its measuring range, so check the specifications, and check availability before ordering.

products.name: OxiPulse Pro Fingertip Pulse Oximeter
products.blurb: A one-button fingertip monitor that shows oxygen saturation and heart rate on a large display. It is a home wellness check, not a substitute for a doctor's reading.
